en: The gray stallion's herd, a thousand mares,
To your Akbaltay who had spoken,
He gave as a reward for the good tidings.
Their lower lips drooping,
Their two humps towering,
Their necks raised like ducks,
Their single humps rising high,
Lumbering, swaying as they walked,
Stepping evenly on all four feet,
Dust covering their long hair—
Four hundred of the nar camels
Jakyp drove up now.
To your elder Akbaltay
He gave them for the good tidings.
Their spreading horns held high,
Milch cows whose milk was rich as butter,
Creatures of great value,
Beyond many of my livestock—
Poor Jakyp, sparing nothing,
Gave four hundred cattle.
“O Akbaltay, elder,
If these words of yours are true,
Take my finest steeds from the horses!
If what I give is too little,
Pour my blood into a leather flask and take it!
If what you say is true,
Leave my file and take my whetstone,
Leave me two and take one,
Leave me in Altai and take my village,
Leave my child and take my wife,
Gather my possessions, take my cloth.
If it will not hurt, O my elder,
Gouge out and take one of my eyes!
I gathered horses without worldly joy,
I amassed much ownerless livestock.
You have brought good tidings;
If what you say is truly true,
Take not only my livestock, but me as well!
At Akbaltay's words,
I am melting away.
Hearing Khan Baltay's words,
Unable to bear my joy,
My heart is burning.
My dear Akbaltay,
If he has been named Manas,
Let me see that child of mine.
Since I came to this Altai,
I had many livestock, but no child;
I suffered for a child.
So that is how it is—the world is shit!
My dear Akbaltay,
You were the one I held to.
God creates life;
Until I see that child,
My life is leaving me!”
So spoke rich Jakyp.
The dwelling was full of (countless) livestock;
When he heard about the child,
The poor soul could not be held in a handspan,
His heart was shaken.
At the words, “You have a child,”
Rich Jakyp, made a poor wretch,
Shed tears from his eyes.
He hurriedly saddled his horse;
Brave Baltay accompanied him.
From the hollow of great Altai,
Along the great river,
When he rode to his home,
Good fortune had come his way.
His senior wife Chyyrdy
Had borne the lion Manas.
While giving birth to Manas,
The senior wife had seen a sign.
When they saw that sign,
Twelve poor women
Died of fright.
The child came down upright;
The old women who saw him doubled over.
Crying, ‘Bar, bar, bar!’
The fierce lord roared and wept.
His blue-black mane stood out;
He came upright upon his feet.
If one looked closely at the child,
The form of a lion appeared.
While she was giving birth to Manas,
Amid the travail God had brought,
There appeared
A white-bearded wandering dervish:
“This child you have borne
Is the youngest of six lions,
A servant beloved of Allah.
His name is Manas, a surpassing lion;
Among mortals given life,
Such a hero has never arisen.
He will whirl his spear and break the ranks;
Whoever fights him will fall to a shot.
He is the champion, he is the lion,
He is the hero, youngest of lions.
If he lives and grows,
He will make roads where none exist,
Attack whoever challenges him.
Eighty-four are fully armed;
If he lives, you will see,
Wherever he strikes is red fire.
Dust cannot catch his stride,
No strength can match his spear thrust;
No mortal can come against him,
No enemy can overcome him.
Renewed whenever brought to an end,
He is Manas, the deeply rooted lion.
Growing stronger whenever he dies,
He is Manas, the commanding hero.
The kakan's Beijing,
If he lives and grows,
He is the hero who will make it stiff with fear.
Bringing uproar and clashing,
Fighting with great Beijing,
There will be no regret in seeing it.
If your valiant Manas grows,
He will bring great strife to the Chinese.
He is the marked one, he is our support;
Living in this world,
He is the renowned lion Manas.
If your valiant son grows,
He will throw the Chinese into turmoil,
Never stopping once he sets his course,
He will stretch his spear toward Beijing.
Against the swarming people,
When they charge and make war,
When they slaughter those whose death is due,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
When they stand face to face,
Striking each other with battle-axes,
When they fight with crashing blows,
When powder spills from the powder-flask,
Their shot and powder exhausted,
When they fight knee to knee,
Utterly despairing of life,
The steel bullet granted by choice—
For waging holy war on unbelievers,
There is no mortal like Manas.
Do as I say:
Before giving the child food,
With this steel bullet, your child—
Let it be the first thing put to his mouth.
Understand my words:
If a shouting enemy comes,
It will surely prove of use;
Sew this into his collar.”
Stroking his forehead three times,
He vanished from sight.
He was a saintly old man himself;
At Manas's birth,
He had come to bless him.
Hardened as a leopard,
Among all the many people
He became known as Khan Manas,
To Jakyp who had had no child.
Gaining a child, he became rich,
Every part of his heart at ease,
Devising plans no one could conceive.
“Jakyp has a child now!” they said.
All the people gathered;
Rich Jakyp began to prepare
A feast for his child.
At that time, champion Jakyp,
With countless livestock but no child,
Now that it was precious to him,
Rich Jakyp had no choice but to give a feast.
“For the people's wishes,” he said,
Now that he had a child,
“It is rich Jakyp's feast,” they said.
Five hundred, beginning with mares,
Saying, “I have a male child,”
Champion Jakyp slaughtered now.
Three hundred, beginning with cows,
He tethered for slaughter.
He slaughtered sheep beyond counting,
Slaughtered sheep in abundance,
Slaughtered rams and held a feast,
Devising plans no one could know.
“It is rich Jakyp's feast,” they said.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
All their people gathered;
Their Torgut assembled to the last one.
Many of rich Jakyp's livestock
Were slaughtered for the feast.
Meat rose like Ala-Too,
Broth spread like Ala-Köl.
Writing a document, setting it down,
They disguised Manas's name,
Named him Chong Jindi.
The Kalmyk village headmen loomed about,
Those in jackets, those with stone rank-badges,
Bustled about gossiping about Jakyp:
“He has fathered Chong Jindi!
Man, this Burut has held a great feast!
Slaughtering livestock like an emperor,
Man, this Burut has grown rich!
He has laid out all his wealth;
Kymyz is nourishment, liquor is nourishment.
Man, we have seen wonders from the Burut,
In these days of our precious lives!
Coming to the Burut's feast,
We have come to see a spectacle indeed.
Sparing no stallions, slaughtering camels,
Slaughtering every kind of stock alike,
Man, this Burut is outstanding!”
Rulers and men with stone rank-badges,
Coming to the feast and eating their fill,
The mighty ones were astonished.
Khan Jakyp had livestock;
The khan of the Black Kalmyks was there.
When my Jakyp held the feast,
All the many people were there.
Devising plans no one could conceive,
For that feast of Manas,
He raced horses and held festivities,
Showing that he was rich.
The dushangs among the Kalmyks
Staggered and stumbled about,
Stayed and settled at the feast,
Drank kymyz and grew heated,
Sweated from their very bones,
Drank liquor and panted,
Their strong men blustered.
So many livestock were slaughtered for the feast;
The child's name became Chong Jindi,
So he was named.
Of the Kalmyks with rank buttons on their caps,
The finest gathered,
As though to see that child.
Each took him in his arms and weighed him,
As though to allot the child a share.
Oshpurbay was close to Jakyp;
Their sheep shared a pen,
Their grain shared a storage pit,
Their food was shared among companions.
When they tended livestock, their labor was shared;
When they milked, their milk was shared.
When the feast for Manas was given,
They gossiped and made an uproar.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus
Raised an uproar among the many people.
Oshpur heard and considered;
The words Oshpurbay heard,
He did not fail to tell Jakyp.
One day the Kalmyks spoke:
“Slaughtering livestock like a ruler,
Laying out all his wealth,
Of the Burut in Altai,
Of this people called Burut,
Slaughtering stock with wealth in full bloom—
This Burut has grown powerful.
These are no ordinary beasts slaughtered;
This is no ordinary Burut.
